name: Cassiterite
spiritual: Connects with earth and ancestral work
physical: Traditionally associated with a feeling of stamina
Crystal healers link it to a sturdy, anchored feeling
summary: Cassiterite is the heavy, dark, glittering tin oxide that launched the Bronze Age, used in tradition for grounding, resolve and steady prosperity.
intro: Cassiterite is a heavy, shiny mineral that looks like black or deep brown glass cut into sharp, stubby prisms and twinned knee shapes. In rare transparent crystals it glows honey-yellow to red-brown with an adamantine fire. It is the main ore of tin, and its density is striking: a fist-sized cluster feels much heavier than it appears. At 6 to 7 on the Mohs scale it is quite hard, so it is durable. Crystal lovers prize it as a grounding stone with a long human history, the stone that made bronze.
history: The name is from the Greek kassiteros, tin. Tin from cassiterite, alloyed with copper, created bronze and defined the Bronze Age, sending traders across Europe and the Mediterranean in search of tin from Cornwall, Spain and beyond. Ancient Phoenicians were said to sail to the Tin Islands for it. Cassiterite is still mined in Bolivia, Malaysia, Indonesia, China and Africa. Its toughness and density helped it accumulate in river gravels, where it was panned like gold. Metaphysical use of cassiterite is recent, and rooted in its heaviness and its association with human innovation.
meaning: Crystal healers regard cassiterite as a stone of grounded strength. Its density and dark color link it to the root chakra, and it is said to support stability, perseverance and practical decision-making. People use it when they need to build something solid, like a business, home or career. Practitioners also associate it with steady prosperity, as it is the stone behind a historical trade. Emotionally it is said to settle worry about security and build resolve. Traditionally it is linked to stamina and steadiness. It is a good choice for those who want a no-nonsense, earthy stone, and pairs well with other metals and minerals.
howToUse: Place a cassiterite cluster on a desk or workbench to support persistent, practical effort. Hold a small piece when you make financial or building decisions. Add it to a grounding grid with smoky quartz and hematite. In meditation, rest it at the base of the spine and breathe into your sense of foundation. A tumbled pocket piece is a heavy, comforting reminder to keep going, one step at a time.
care: Cassiterite is hard, dense and stable. Rinse in lukewarm water and dry with a soft cloth when needed. It tolerates sunlight and most cleansing methods, such as sound, smoke, moonlight and brief sun. Avoid strong acids. Store separately from softer minerals, since it can scratch them, and be careful with clusters, as thin edges may chip.
identify: Genuine cassiterite is exceptionally heavy for its size, with an adamantine luster and a pale brown to white streak. It forms stubby tetragonal crystals and twinned knees. It is often confused with black tourmaline, sphalerite, garnet and wolframite. Tourmaline is lighter and striated, sphalerite has cleavage, and wolframite is more metallic and bladed. Fakes are rare, but resin-cast black pieces occasionally appear. Weight is a good clue.
